title: Onboarding
text:
Our on-boarding process is heavily inspired by Kirstie Whittacre’s Lab group. On-boarding aims to:

Complete a minimum example of using git and github, by;
Writing a short member profile.
Investing some time in the lab group.

This process also serves to create a front end directory of lab members, building our community over time.
In order to “on-board”, please complete the following technical steps:

Install git on your local machine.
Clone a copy of this website repo and create a new branch.
Name the branch as firstname-lastname (e.g. ed-palmer)
Add a profile page as a .qmd document in the people folder:

Use a category of “active lab member” in the yaml header of the file.
Take a look at any of the other profiles for examples.

Push your branch to github.
Submit a pull request on github.

This will complete the technical aspects of on-boarding. You will have learnt through this process, all the vital steps that we will be using for sharing code and completing project peer review. If it feels daunting, please do not worry. We are all here to help you with this process.
Beyond this, new members are expected to:

Read and understand the lab charter, and follow our code of conduct.
Contribute your knowledge and experience to others in the lab (as we will do with you.)

We look forward to seeing you in the lab!

title: Ed Palmer
text:
I am a consultant in anaesthesia and intensive care medicine based in London, UK. My research background is in the reuse of routinely collected longitudinal healthcare data for research. My interests are directed towards research goals that may be challenging to meet under traditional frameworks because anticipated effect sizes are very small, that it is too expensive to run a classical trial, or there are concerns over equipoise. My PhD investigated the safe limits—including addressing intrinsic biases—of these resources. This ties with my clinical interest in sepsis, where my research took steps towards a better understanding of “time zero” and the association between physiological trajectories and outcomes in sepsis.
I started this lab group as a way to bring together and support like minded individuals, improve local patient care using data informed methods, and engage with research in a positive way.
The lab group name “The Data Science Breakfast Club” is a loving nod to my long time friend and mentor Prof. Steve Harris, who started a club by the same name more than a decade ago. It was through meeting Steve that my love for this subject florished, and in many respects, this is my attempt at paying it forward.
As a past fellow of the Software Sustainability Institute, I am a strong proponent of open data, reproducible research and free1 and open software. When I am not tinkering with ventilators or R, I can usually be found running, reading and watching science fiction, or going on adventures with my wonderful children.

title: Laxative review
section: A systematic review of laxative use in critically unwell patients: Are we doing more harm than good?
text:
A systematic review of laxative use in critically unwell patients: Are we doing more harm than good?

Diarrhoea is common in critically unwell patients and is associated with prolonged intensive care unit (ICU) stay and increased mortality. Its causes are multifactorial; however, emerging evidence suggests that laxative exposure may be an important, and potentially modifiable, contributor. Laxatives are frequently prescribed in ICU patients to prevent constipation, increasingly as part of bowel management protocols (BMP) and care bundles, despite limited supporting evidence. This systematic review evaluated the effects and prevailing associations of laxatives on clinical outcomes in critically unwell adults.

title: Code of Conduct
text:
This code of conduct is adapted from The Whitaker Lab code of conduct, which we consider gold standard.
We value the participation of every member of our community and want to ensure that every contributor has an enjoyable and fulfilling experience. Accordingly, everyone who participates in any DataSciBC project is expected to show respect and courtesy to other community members at all time.
Ed Palmer, as head of the DataSciBC (aka “Palmer-Lab”), and all lab members, are dedicated to a positive, respectful, and harassment-free experience for everyone, regardless of gender, gender identity and expression, sexual orientation, disability, physical appearance, body size, race, age or religion.
As a community, we do not tolerate bullying or harassment by and/or of members of our community in any form.
We are particularly motivated to support new and/or anxious collaborators, those who would consider themselves under-represented in our field, and anyone at any stage who are looking to learn and develop new skills.
To make clear what is expected, we ask all members of the community to conform to the following Code of Conduct:

All communication—online and in person—should be appropriate for a professional audience including people of many different backgrounds.
Be respectful to others. Do not insult or put down other contributors. It can take a lot of courage to showcase your work to others and await critical feedback. We seek to make that experience a positive one.

To report an issue please contact Ed Palmer. All communication will be treated as confidential.


This sentence is stolen from Bastian Greshake’s email footer and forms the basis of the DataSciBC’s policy on flexible working:

While I may be sending this email outside my normal office hours, I have no expectation to receive a reply outside yours.

The hours that members of the lab choose to put in is up to them. This is a voluntary endeavour, and we understand that time is both a valuable and precious commodity. We are each welcome to send work-related communications or pull requests over the weekend or late at night, but no lab members are required or expected to reply to them outside of “typical” working hours. The DataSciBC maintains a whatsapp group for more casual communication, and these same principles apply. Members are welcome to mute, or even leave and rejoin when convenient.
Ideally, all lab members will have some time each week to overlap with Ed in order to stay in touch on any challenges or successes. The Thursday morning meeting is the best opportunity for this.

title: Lab Charter
text:
“Scientia per communionem” (knowledge through fellowship) emphasises the founding ethos of our lab group: collaboration, learning, and sharing of knowledge for the benefit of all.
Much like the medical firm (now lost to time) the academic lab group is a wonderful, shared community. It brings together like minded individuals on a journey to better themselves and expand their knowledge. It provides a solid core that persists for members as they move between placements, careers or even countries.
Why have a charter? Over time, labs mature and often develop their own scientific “political” leanings. In our experience, this can contribute to the negative interface between science (the method of learning) and academia (the human implementation of that method). Put another way, “successful” labs are often not defined by the quality of their scientific discovery, but by their ability to deluge the market with thematic papers and control the narrative around “their” subject. We aim to redefine what success looks like in medical academia. By building a charter, we can hold ourselves accountable to the standards we have chosen to set. We aim to be an aspirational force, with scientific discovery at its core. This requires a fundamental honesty: that we do not know, are not an authority, and can and will be wrong.

title: Lab Charter
text:
Core Principles

Knowledge can never be owned, only shared[1].
A successful fellow is a successful lab; lift each other up.
Individual differences are to be celebrated and respected. We are united by a passion for acquiring and sharing knowledge.
Extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence; all opinions are provisional and can be falsified by further experimentation and study.
Be ruthless in experimental planning and design. Never build a study because the data was there and it was convenient.
If it isn’t replicable, it didn’t happen.

title: Peri-Met study
section: Peri-Met Study: peripheral metaraminol in septic shock
text:
Peri-Met Study: peripheral metaraminol in septic shock

Septic shock is a life-threatening complication of infection in which blood pressure falls dangerously low. Treatment often includes medicines called vasopressors, which raise blood pressure by narrowing the blood vessels. Increasingly, these are started through a standard drip in the arm rather than waiting for a larger “central” line to be placed.
In the UK, the medicine most often used this way is metaraminol. International guidelines recommend a different drug, noradrenaline, and the two have never been compared directly in a clinical trial in septic shock.
The Peri-Met Study aims to address this gap. We are first reviewing the published evidence, and will use this to inform on whether or not a small pilot trial at the Whittington Hospital would be appropriate. The pilot will test whether a larger, multicentre trial is feasible.

title: Creatine study
section: Creatine and recovery from critical illness
text:
Creatine and recovery from critical illness

Many people who survive a stay in intensive care leave hospital much weaker than before. They can lose a striking amount of muscle in the first week or two, and for some the weakness lasts months or years. It affects how well they can walk, work and look after themselves. There are still no proven treatments beyond rehabilitation and good nutrition.
Creatine is a natural compound that helps muscles store and supply energy. As a supplement it is cheap, widely available and well studied. In healthy adults and older people, adding it to exercise can modestly improve muscle mass and strength. Whether that holds after critical illness is unknown, and the early research is limited and mixed.
We are carrying out a systematic review of all the published evidence and registered trials of creatine in critical illness and recovery. We want to find out what is already known, where the evidence is weakest, and whether creatine deserves a properly designed clinical trial. In particular, we are asking when during recovery it is most likely to help.

text:
I am an FY4 doctor currently working in intensive care in London. I’ll be moving to ED next year and ultimately plan on training in anaesthetics. I would also like to do more voluntary work in the future, having done some in Bulgaria last year. 
I am particularly interested in day case surgery, which I have worked to promote from both anaesthetic and surgical perspectives, and pain management, which was the subject of my PGCert. I care about anything that will improve my patients’ experiences, though, and am always involved in quality improvement.

I am passionate about clinical research, having completed the Academic Foundation Programme (AFP), and I continue to pursue research alongside my clinical training.
